strengths: Addresses a well-motivated and practically relevant problem: the inference latency of autoregressive structured-language models for 3D perception. The core result—roughly 5x decoding speedup at equal or slightly better F1 on ASE (e.g., 382 ms vs. 75 ms at ~0.91 F1)—is a genuine and useful efficiency contribution.

The method is described clearly and is technically sound: multi-token prediction heads with decaying loss weights, shared projection/token/confidence heads, a numerical-token distance criterion for structured language, and two complementary filtering strategies (SSD and CGD) are all specified with equations and diagrams (Figs. 3, 4).

Evaluation is reasonably thorough for the chosen task: two public benchmarks (ASE, Structured3D), val and test splits, comparisons against retrained SceneScript, naive MTP at n = 4/8/10, and a specialized layout method (RoomFormer), plus parameter/latency/accepted-token metrics.

Ablations (Table 3) are informative and support the design choices: they isolate the effect of the distance threshold tau, the head-sharing mechanism (43% parameter reduction), and the proposed CGD versus ProductThre/SoftmaxThre. Figs. 7 and 8 provide useful diagnostic analysis (acceptance distributions and the observation that softmax scores do not reliably indicate token reliability).

Reproducibility is comparatively good: dataset splits, decoder architecture (8 layers, 512-dim, 8 heads), optimizer, learning rates, batch size, training epochs, and loss weights are all reported, and the datasets are public.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. Multi-token prediction, self-speculative decoding, confidence-based acceptance, and weight-shared prediction heads are all existing components (Gloeckle et al.; Leviathan et al.; Stern et al.; Medusa; DeepSeek-V3; VocalNet). The contribution is largely an adaptation/combination of these for structured 3D language models, with CGD being a modest variant of learned-confidence acceptance.

The headline "12.04% higher F1" and "43% fewer parameters" are measured against a naive SceneScript + MTP baseline that the authors themselves trained; the gain over the actual prior method (SceneScript) is much smaller (~1.5-2 F1 points on ASE, ~1.7 on Structured3D). The framing overstates the improvement relative to the true state of the art.

The decoding-strategy baselines are weak. Only ProductThre and SoftmaxThre are compared for token filtering; well-known alternatives such as Medusa-style typical acceptance, EAGLE, and draft-model speculative decoding are cited but not evaluated, so it is unclear whether CGD is competitive with the broader literature.

The efficiency framing omits an important trade-off: naive SceneScript + MTP is actually faster than Fast SceneScript at the same head count (54 ms vs. 75 ms at n = 10 on ASE; 154 ms vs. 211 ms on Structured3D). The paper's advantage is accuracy at a given head count, which should be stated more directly.

Evaluation is narrow: only 3D layout estimation on two indoor datasets. The paper claims generality to 3D object detection and 3D object part reconstruction, and positions itself as a general framework, but provides no experiments on those tasks; comparisons with other language-based generalists (e.g., SpatialLLM) are also absent.

Minor reporting inconsistencies reduce confidence in the numbers: Fig. 1 plots Fast SceneScript at ~55 ms and ~0.92 F1 with an annotation of "5.09x faster," which corresponds to the 75 ms/382 ms pair in Table 1 rather than the plotted point; the plotted F1 (~0.92) also does not exactly match the 0.910/0.913 values in Table 1.

The additional training cost of the MTP stage (NTP 60 epochs followed by MTP 30 epochs) and its sensitivity to the loss weights lambda_h and lambda_c and to the confidence threshold epsilon are not analyzed, which matters for practical adoption.

strengths: Addresses an important efficiency bottleneck in autoregressive structured language models for 3D scene layout estimation, showing that multi-token prediction can be made accurate with token filtering.
Delivers strong empirical efficiency gains: up to 5.09x faster decoding than SceneScript on ASE and 5.57x/4.58x faster on Structured3D while maintaining or improving F1-Score.
Proposes two effective token filtering strategies: SSD adapted with a distance metric for numerical tokens, and confidence-guided decoding (CGD) that predicts token reliability on the fly.

Introduces a parameter-efficient mechanism that substantially reduces parameter overhead relative to naive SceneScript+MTP, e.g., from 23.67M to 15.05M for n=8 and from 26.43M to 15.05M for n=10 with SSD.
Ablation studies are thorough, comparing SSD, CGD, ProductThre, SoftmaxThre, and with/without parameter sharing, and include useful token-acceptance and confidence-distribution analyses.
The paper is clearly written and well organized, with informative figures and detailed implementation settings such as datasets, splits, optimizer, epochs, loss weights, and architecture dimensions.
The qualitative results on ASE and Structured3D show more complete and accurate scene layouts compared to SceneScript+MTP, supporting the practical usefulness of the method.
weaknesses: Evaluation is limited to 3D indoor layout estimation on ASE and Structured3D; despite claiming a general framework, no experiments are shown on other 3D perception tasks such as object detection or 3D object part reconstruction.

The critical CGD threshold epsilon is not specified in the main text, making exact reproduction of the proposed confidence-guided decoding difficult; τ is reported but the confidence threshold is missing.

The abstract claims only ~7.5% additional parameters compared to SceneScript, but the main CGD variant uses 16.10M parameters versus 14.00M (~15% overhead); the 7.5% figure applies to the SSD variant, not CGD.

The parameter-efficient mechanism is not fully explained: it is unclear how a shared projection block and shared token head can generate distinct hidden states for different future tokens, and Figure 3 appears to show per-head projection blocks, creating ambiguity.

CGD training labels are derived from agreement between head i and the first head rather than ground-truth correctness, so the confidence head may learn self-consistency instead of true token reliability; calibration and theoretical justification are limited.
Only MTP and two scoring-based filtering baselines are compared; broader acceleration paradigms such as quantization, pruning, distillation, or separate-draft speculative decoding are not evaluated.

Some numerical claims are not directly verifiable from the tables, e.g., the reported 12.04% F1 improvement and the 43% parameter reduction are specific to certain settings and are not consistently supported across the main results.
No code release or error bars/statistical significance tests are provided, which weakens reproducibility and confidence in small performance differences.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and practically important bottleneck: autoregressive next-token prediction in structured-language perception models (SceneScript) is slow, and a 5× latency reduction on ASE/Structured3D with maintained F1 is a useful practical result.

The empirical observation that structured perception language is highly predictable—average accepted tokens α≈9 per decoder pass with n=8–10 heads (Table 1, Table 3)—is interesting and could motivate follow-up work on decoding for structured-language models.

The system is reasonably engineered: the head-sharing mechanism with a lightweight projection block reduces decoder parameters (Table 3, row i vs. row j: 16.10M vs. 31.03M, ~48% fewer) with comparable F1, and the ablation in Table 3 systematically compares SSD (τ=0/2/5), ProductThre, SoftmaxThre, and CGD.

The paper is generally clearly written, with implementation details (8-layer decoder, 512-dim, 8 heads, AdamW, lr=0.001, λh=0.8, λc=0.5, τ=2, 60/30/600 epochs) that support reproducibility, plus qualitative comparisons (Figs. 5–6) and analysis of softmax-score distributions (Fig. 8).
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core ingredients are all existing: multi-token prediction (Gloeckle et al., 2024), self-speculative decoding (Leviathan et al., 2023), confidence-head verification (Medusa, Cai et al., 2024), and scoring-based token filtering (Liu et al., 2025; Nie et al., 2025). CGD is essentially a Medusa-style confidence head trained to predict agreement with the first head, and the head-sharing scheme is a small engineering variant. The contribution is largely an application/combination of prior acceleration techniques to one model, not a fundamentally new decoding paradigm.

The accuracy claim is supported by inconsistent baselines. Table 1 reports SceneScript (retrained) at ASE val mean F1 = 0.891, whereas Table 3 reports SceneScript at 0.913 on the same val set (with a different latency, 375 vs. 382 ms). Fast SceneScript (SSD/CGD) is 0.911–0.912, i.e., below the 0.913 number in the paper's own ablation. Thus 'comparable or even better' accuracy depends on which baseline is used, and the headline '12.04% higher F1-Score' (Fig. 1, Sec. 4.3) is computed against a degraded SceneScript+MTP baseline rather than the NTP model—overstating the accuracy contribution.

No comparison against directly relevant acceleration baselines (Medusa, EAGLE, lookahead decoding, DynaMo, etc.), which are cited but not evaluated; the scoring-based baselines (ProductThre/SoftmaxThre) are re-implementations whose thresholds (0.3/0.5) may disadvantage them. This makes it hard to assess whether the proposed filtering is genuinely better than the state of the art in speculative decoding.

The paper reports that MTP+filtering improves F1 over the NTP baseline (e.g., 0.912 vs. 0.891 in Table 1), which is counterintuitive, yet provides no analysis or explanation (regularization from the MTP loss? the τ tolerance on numeric tokens? run-to-run noise?). Without seeds/variance, this central 'accurate' claim is not substantiated.

The distance-based reliability criterion for numeric tokens (Eq. 3, τ=2) is not justified with respect to the evaluation unit (F1 computed at 5 cm intervals). Accepting tokens that deviate from the verified value by up to τ could interact with the metric, and no sensitivity analysis ties τ to physical error or to F1 degradation. This also makes the comparison with the NTP baseline less clean, since it changes the effective acceptance criterion.

Claims of generality ('perception-generalist', potential for 3D object detection/reconstruction) are not tested; all experiments are limited to 3D layout estimation on two indoor datasets, and RoomFormer is the only specialized baseline. The versatility claim therefore remains unsupported.

Efficiency evaluation is thin: latency is measured only on a single GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) without breaking out the token-filtering overhead or reporting memory/throughput; no statistical significance or variance is reported for any metric.

strengths: Addresses a practically important problem: autoregressive next-token inference in language-based 3D scene understanding is slow, and the paper proposes a targeted acceleration framework.

Introduces multi-token prediction (MTP) to structured language for 3D scenes and develops two token-filtering strategies: adapted self-speculative decoding (SSD) with a numerical-token distance metric and confidence-guided decoding (CGD).

Provides extensive experiments on ASE, Structured3D, and SceneCAD for layout estimation and object detection, including ablations on number of heads, filtering thresholds, distance tolerance τ, confidence supervision, and parameter sharing.

Demonstrates substantial speedups over SceneScript and improved accuracy over naive MTP baselines, while reducing parameter overhead relative to MTP through head sharing and a parameter-efficient projection block.
Qualitative comparisons and distribution analyses of accepted tokens/softmax scores help support the effectiveness of the token-filtering mechanisms.
The paper is generally well organized, with supplementary material covering implementation details, additional ablations, failure cases, and qualitative results.
weaknesses: Novelty is limited: MTP, self-speculative decoding, and confidence-based thresholding already exist; adapting them to structured language for 3D scenes is largely an engineering combination. The proposed CGD is essentially a learned confidence head and is not convincingly superior to SSD, which often matches or exceeds it in speed and accuracy in the main tables.

The parameter-efficient mechanism is technically unclear. The paper states that a shared projection block is applied to f_{k+1} to generate distinct hidden states for n future tokens, but if the same input and shared weights are used, it is unclear how the hidden states remain distinct; the paper does not explain whether the block is applied recursively, with position-specific modulation, or in another way. This affects reproducibility and understanding of why head sharing works.

Reproducibility is limited: no code release is mentioned, the numerical-token distance metric is not fully specified, and the projection-block input/usage is ambiguous. Object detection on ASE uses bounding boxes generated by TR3D from MMDection3D rather than human-verified ground truth, which weakens the validity of those object-detection results.

Some numerical claims in the abstract and Figure 1 do not align cleanly with the main tables. For example, the 12.04% F1 improvement, 43% fewer parameters, and 7.5% additional parameters appear to mix SSD and CGD variants; the 'up to 9 tokens' claim comes from SSD, not the proposed CGD, which accepts fewer tokens on average.

Evaluation breadth is limited: only SceneScript is accelerated as the base architecture, and there is no comparison to other acceleration approaches such as Medusa, draft-model speculative decoding, or alternative MTP variants. The method is also slower than naive MTP, so it does not uniformly improve the speed-accuracy tradeoff.

The claim that CGD provides on-the-fly decoding by removing verification delay is not well supported: CGD is slower than SSD in Tables 1-3 despite SSD's verification step, and its accuracy advantage is marginal or absent on ASE validation. This weakens the motivation for CGD over the simpler SSD alternative.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and important bottleneck in language-based 3D scene understanding: autoregressive next-token prediction is slow. The proposed Fast SceneScript reduces decoder iterations via multi-token prediction and reports substantial speedups, e.g., 5.14× faster inference for 3D object detection and ~5.09× for layout estimation, while maintaining or improving accuracy in several settings.

The technical design is reasonable and well motivated: adapting self-speculative decoding (SSD) to structured language with a numerical distance metric, proposing confidence-guided decoding (CGD) with learned confidence heads, and introducing a parameter-efficient sharing mechanism that reduces MTP parameter overhead by ~43% compared with standard MTP. The ablations in Table 4 and supplementary tables support the effectiveness of these components.

Experiments are relatively thorough for the chosen scope: layout estimation on ASE, Structured3D, and SceneCAD, plus object detection on ASE and SceneCAD. The paper includes ablations on the number of MTP heads, token filtering strategies, thresholds τ and ε, confidence supervision variants, and qualitative comparisons, which strengthens the empirical claims.

The writing is generally clear, the method is described with useful diagrams, and the supplementary material provides additional implementation details, dataset split names, and architecture descriptions, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental. Multi-token prediction, speculative decoding, and token filtering are existing ideas from the LLM literature; the main novelty here is their adaptation to structured language models for 3D scenes and the confidence-guided decoding variant. This is a practical engineering contribution rather than a fundamentally new method.

The confidence target in CGD is based on consistency with the first head rather than ground-truth correctness. If the first head is confidently wrong, the confidence head may still assign high reliability to incorrect tokens. The supplementary material compares a ground-truth-supervised variant and reports comparable accuracy, but the default self-consistency target remains a conceptual weakness for a token-filtering reliability mechanism.

The parameter-efficient head-sharing mechanism is not fully specified. The paper says the token/confidence heads and projection block are shared across all n future-token heads, but it is unclear how distinct hidden states and distinct token predictions are generated for different future positions. This is important for understanding and reproducing the method, and the explanation is ambiguous in both the main text and Fig. 3.

The numerical token distance threshold τ=2 lacks units and scale. It is not clear whether the tokens are continuous values, discretized bins, normalized coordinates, or something else, making the distance-based reliability check difficult to reproduce and potentially dataset-specific.

Some speedup numbers are inconsistently presented. For example, the abstract and introduction claim 5.09× speedup for layout estimation, but Table 1 shows several different speedups depending on the configuration (e.g., 387 ms vs 92 ms is about 4.2×, while 387 ms vs 75 ms is about 5.2×). The paper should more carefully specify which configuration each headline number refers to.

Evaluation is limited to indoor 3D scene understanding (layout estimation and object detection) on three datasets. Generality to outdoor scenes, other perception tasks, or larger-scale real-world settings is not demonstrated. Comparisons are mainly against SceneScript and SceneScript+MTP, with limited comparison to other efficient decoding or inference acceleration methods beyond simple thresholding baselines.

strengths: Addresses a relevant problem: the high inference latency of autoregressive structured language models for 3D scene understanding, and applies multi-token prediction (MTP) to SceneScript in a way that is, to my knowledge, novel for this domain.

Reports substantial empirical speedups: roughly 5x faster layout estimation and object detection on ASE, Structured3D, and SceneCAD while maintaining or slightly improving F1 scores, supported by main tables and qualitative comparisons.

Adapts self-speculative decoding (SSD) to structured language by introducing a distance-based acceptance criterion for numerical tokens; the ablation shows that τ=2 improves accepted token count without degrading F1 on ASE val.

Proposes a parameter-efficient head/projection sharing mechanism that reduces parameters relative to vanilla MTP variants (e.g., about 43% fewer parameters than MTP-10 in some settings), with ablations on parameter count and accuracy.
Includes useful supplementary material: hyperparameters, dataset splits, network architecture details, additional ablations, failure cases, and analyses of softmax-score distributions.

The paper is generally well organized and readable, with clear motivation, illustrative figures (e.g., inference iteration comparison, token filtering strategies), and comparisons to relevant baselines.
weaknesses: The core MTP architecture is ambiguously described and potentially inconsistent: the text states that a shared projection block is applied to f_{k+1} to generate distinct hidden states f_{k+i} for i∈[2,n], and that the projection/token/confidence heads are shared across all n tokens. With the same input and shared parameters, a deterministic shared block cannot produce distinct predictions for different future tokens unless the block is applied recursively or has token-index-specific inputs, which is not specified. This undermines technical soundness and reproducibility.

The proposed confidence-guided decoding (CGD) is not shown to be superior to the simpler adapted SSD. In Table 1 (n=8), SSD is faster than CGD (81 ms vs. 92 ms) and has equal or slightly better F1 (0.912 vs. 0.911 on val; 0.913 vs. 0.913 on test). Similar trends appear for n=10 and other datasets. Thus a main contribution lacks clear empirical justification.

The confidence head is trained to predict agreement with the first head, not correctness. If the first head is wrong and other heads agree, CGD may accept unreliable tokens. The paper reports only end-task F1 and does not provide token-level precision/recall, calibration, or false-accept analysis for the filtering strategies.

Object detection evaluation on ASE uses pseudo-labels generated by TR3D rather than ground-truth bounding boxes. This weakens the object detection claims and may not reflect true 3D object detection performance.

Novelty is incremental: MTP and speculative decoding are existing techniques, and their adaptation to SceneScript is largely an engineering contribution. The paper does not compare against stronger MTP acceleration baselines such as Medusa or tree-based speculative decoding methods.

The parameter claim is inconsistent: the abstract says the method adds only ~7.5% additional parameters, but CGD adds ~15% over SceneScript (16.10M vs. 14.00M). The claimed ~43% reduction is relative to MTP-10, not to the base model, and varies across configurations.
Evaluation lacks error bars, multiple runs, or statistical significance testing. Latency is measured on a single GPU (RTX 2080 Ti) without variance or sensitivity analysis across hardware.

Key hyperparameters (τ=2, ε=0.90, λ_h=0.8) are tuned on ASE val, and generalization to other datasets is not thoroughly analyzed. The distance threshold for numerical tokens may be dataset- or unit-dependent.

The paper claims to be the first to introduce MTP to language-based perception models, but this claim is not fully verified and broader related work on multi-token/multi-head decoding and multimodal MTP is not discussed or compared.
No code or pretrained models are mentioned for release, limiting reproducibility. Some architectural details remain unclear even after reading the supplementary material.
